prompt.context: Our client, Chicouver Cycle (pronounced 'Chai-cover'), is a bikesharing startup. Like other bikeshare operators in cities around the world, Chicouver Cycle owns bicycles and rents them out to users one trip at a time.
prompt.question: Chicouver Cycle wants to know how they should launch operations in the city of Chicouver. They have specifically asked us to recommend one or more of Chicouver's neighborhoods to enter.

clarifying_info.a: Chicouver residents are avid bicyclists. The city is also a popular tourist destination.

clarifying_info.q: Is there existing competition in the bikeshare market?
clarifying_info.a: There is currently no existing bikeshare system in Chicouver.

clarifying_info.q: What are the client's financial goals?
clarifying_info.a: Our client wants to generate cash from initial launch to fund further growth. Profitability is important.

clarifying_info.q: What does the client charge per trip, and what system models are being considered?
clarifying_info.a: Most bikeshare systems charge $1 per trip; our client will charge the same. The client is choosing between two models: docking and dockless.
The city of Chicouver has worked with other sharing economy platforms before; permitting will not be an issue.
Chicouver has reasonable weather for biking all year round.

exhibits.title: Chicouver's Neighborhoods
exhibits.shows: A map of Chicouver showing seven named neighborhoods with population density shading (low to high) and a 1-mile scale bar. Each neighborhood has a brief descriptor label.

neighborhoods: Swanville: Ritzy residential neighborhood, home to Chicouver's titans of industry
Bayside Heights: Chicouver's main tourist district
Capitol Hill: Popular with locals Monday through Saturday
Historic District: Chicouver's main tourist district
Nightlife District: Popular with locals Monday through Saturday
Recreation District: Gyms, museums, nature parks frequented by local residents after work
CBD: Business district where all of Chicouver's residents commute to work

exhibits.title: Chicouver's Topography
exhibits.shows: A map of Chicouver with the same neighborhood layout as Exhibit A, now shaded by topography from flat to very hilly.

data.topography_notes: Neighborhoods vary from flat to moderately hilly to very hilly; the historic/tourist district appears very hilly.

exhibits.title: Projections by Type of Bikeshare Trip
exhibits.shows: A table with four trip types (Commuting, Tourism, Recreation, Nightlife) showing projected weekly trips, number of bikes needed to meet demand, and utilization percentage.

data.note: Utilization = # hours bike is used each week / total # hours in a week

exhibits.title: Bikeshare Systems
exhibits.shows: A comparison of two bikeshare system types: Docking (users must start and end trips at a docking station) vs. Dockless (users pick up any available bike and end a trip anywhere within the service area).

data.Docking: Users must start and end trips at a docking station.
data.Dockless: Users pick up any available bike and end a trip anywhere within the service area.

exhibits.title: Projected Costs
exhibits.shows: A cost table comparing docking vs. dockless systems across three cost line items: annual cost per bike, annual cost per docking station, and annual distribution cost per bike under three terrain types (flat, moderately hilly, very hilly).

framework: Overall Market: Identify target customers (residents vs. tourists) and their preferences; assess substitutes (car, transit, walking); evaluate economic trends in Chicouver affecting sharing economy adoption
Our Client: Assess core competencies and prior city launch experience; understand brand/image; determine desired leanness at launch and future growth aspirations (other products/services)
Profitability: Estimate revenues (user volume, trip frequency, $1/trip price) and costs (bikes, docking equipment if applicable, distribution/rebalancing labor, technology, marketing)

Location Choice: Evaluate neighborhoods on population density, neighborhood use type (residential vs. commercial vs. tourist), household income, and critically topography (hilly terrain increases distribution costs and reduces ridership)

questions.prompt: Analyze Exhibits A and B: which neighborhoods are most attractive and why? What types of trips occur in Chicouver?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that there are 3 residential neighborhoods (Swanville, Capitol Hill, Bayside Heights) whose residents commute to CBD. After work, residents travel from CBD to Recreation and Nightlife Districts. Tourists stay within the Historic District. Topography matters: flat terrain reduces costs and encourages ridership. Candidate should map trip flows: Commuting (residential to CBD), Tourism (within Historic District), Recreation (CBD to Recreation District), Nightlife (CBD to Nightlife District). Should flag that terrain drives both revenue attractiveness and cost structure.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit C, analyze the four trip types. Which appear most and least efficient?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that Tourism and Recreation have high utilization (24% and 22%) with few bikes needed (5K and 4K), suggesting capital efficiency. Commuting and Nightlife have very low utilization (4% and 7%) despite needing many bikes (50K and 30K), making them capital-intensive. High trip volume alone does not make a trip type attractive if it requires a large fleet with low utilization.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibits D and E, calculate annual profit for each trip type under both docking and dockless systems. Assume 50 weeks per year and $1 per trip. Use flat terrain for Commuting and Nightlife, moderately hilly for Recreation, and very hilly for Tourism.
questions.guidance: Candidate should methodically compute revenue, bike cost, station cost (docking only), and distribution cost for each trip type and system. Key insight: dockless eliminates station costs but doubles distribution costs; on flat terrain the savings dominate (nightlife), while on very hilly terrain the doubled distribution cost is punishing (tourism).

math.setup: Revenue = $1 × (trips per week in thousands × 1000) × 50 weeks. Bike cost = $200 × (bikes in thousands × 1000). Station count = bikes / 20; Station cost = $10,000 × stations (docking only). Distribution cost = dist_cost_per_bike × bikes.
steps: COMMUTING (flat terrain, 500K trips/week, 50K bikes): Revenue = $1 × 500K × 50 = $25M. Bike cost = $200 × 50K = $10M. Stations = 50K/20 = 2,500; Station cost = 2,500 × $10K = $25M. Docking dist cost = $100 × 50K = $5M. Dockless dist cost = $200 × 50K = $10M. Docking profit = 25 – 10 – 25 – 5 = –$15M. Dockless profit = 25 – 10 – 10 = +$5M.

TOURISM (very hilly, 400K trips/week, 5K bikes): Revenue = $1 × 400K × 50 = $20M. Bike cost = $200 × 5K = $1M. Stations = 5K/20 = 250; Station cost = 250 × $10K = $2.5M. Docking dist cost = $2,000 × 5K = $10M. Dockless dist cost = $4,000 × 5K = $20M. Docking profit = 20 – 1 – 2.5 – 10 = +$6.5M. Dockless profit = 20 – 1 – 20 = –$1M.

RECREATION (moderately hilly, 300K trips/week, 4K bikes): Revenue = $1 × 300K × 50 = $15M. Bike cost = $200 × 4K = $0.8M. Stations = 4K/20 = 200; Station cost = 200 × $10K = $2M. Docking dist cost = $500 × 4K = $2M. Dockless dist cost = $1,000 × 4K = $4M. Docking profit = 15 – 0.8 – 2 – 2 = +$10.2M. Dockless profit = 15 – 0.8 – 4 = +$10.2M.

NIGHTLIFE (flat, 600K trips/week, 30K bikes): Revenue = $1 × 600K × 50 = $30M. Bike cost = $200 × 30K = $6M. Stations = 30K/20 = 1,500; Station cost = 1,500 × $10K = $15M. Docking dist cost = $100 × 30K = $3M. Dockless dist cost = $200 × 30K = $6M. Docking profit = 30 – 6 – 15 – 3 = +$6M. Dockless profit = 30 – 6 – 6 = +$18M.
math.answer: Summary of annual profits — Commuting: Docking –$15M, Dockless +$5M. Tourism: Docking +$6.5M, Dockless –$1M. Recreation: Docking +$10.2M, Dockless +$10.2M. Nightlife: Docking +$6M, Dockless +$18M. Best option: Dockless system in Nightlife District at +$18M annual profit.

questions.exhibit_ref: Exhibit C, Exhibit D, Exhibit E

recommendation: Chicouver Cycle should launch a dockless bikeshare system targeting the Nightlife District, generating an estimated $18M in annual profit.

Dockless eliminates $15M in docking station costs relative to a docking system, while only adding $3M in additional distribution costs thanks to the Nightlife District's flat terrain — a net gain of $12M.
The Nightlife District has the highest trip volume (600K/week), making it the most revenue-rich entry point despite relatively low utilization (7%).
risks: Utilization for nightlife trips is low (7%), meaning the large bike fleet sits idle most of the time, increasing per-trip economics sensitivity to demand fluctuations.
Dockless systems can lead to bike clutter or poor redistribution if users leave bikes in inconvenient locations, raising operational costs.
As Chicouver Cycle grows, other sharing economy competitors or additional bikeshare entrants may enter the market and erode margins.
next_steps: Explore cross-utilization: the Recreation District is geographically adjacent to the Nightlife District. Using the same bike fleet to serve recreation trips (daytime) and nightlife trips (evening) could significantly improve utilization and margins.
Investigate demand-side incentives to reduce distribution costs — for example, rewarding users who end trips at high-demand locations, reducing the need for manual redistribution.
Build customer loyalty and switching costs (subscription plans, loyalty rewards, app stickiness) to defend against future competitive entry.
As cash flows stabilize, evaluate expansion to other trip types — the dockless model will maintain cost advantages in flat-terrain neighborhoods.
